Most KOL Campaigns Are Expensive Screenshots of Impressions.

Growth · Crypto

The standard Web3 creator report looks impressive until someone asks what changed.

It contains follower counts, views, engagement rates, screenshots, and a list of posts. It may demonstrate that content was published and attention occurred. It rarely proves that the campaign improved understanding, attracted the right participants, changed product behavior, or created commercial value.

This is not only a measurement problem. It begins with how creators are selected and what they are asked to do.

InfoFi turned attention into a score. Then the rules changed.

The creator market changed quickly. Kaito introduced Yaps in late 2024, and by 2025 projects were competing for mindshare across leaderboards and incentive programs. Cookie Snaps and Wallchain offered variations on the same underlying proposition: measure contribution to the conversation, reward participation and make influence more legible to buyers. The attraction was obvious. Brands could reach beyond a handful of expensive KOL retainers, and smaller creators had a route into campaigns. But a rising mindshare score was still not evidence of a user installing a wallet or making a useful transaction. Background: the emergence of InfoFi.

On 15 January 2026, X moved to revoke API access for apps paying people to post. Kaito discontinued Yaps and incentivized leaderboards and shifted toward selected brand–creator work through Kaito Studio; Cookie shut down Snaps. This was a platform-dependency shock as much as a verdict on low-quality engagement. A rewards system can coordinate attention, but it cannot treat access to somebody else's feed or API as permanent infrastructure. Kaito's pivot; InfoFi's January reset.

The measurement problem did not disappear when the leaderboards did. Attention, distribution and product adoption are still three different things.

OPERATOR OBSERVATION · PRIOR WEB3 GROWTH WORK

In previous wallet growth roles, creator promotion, quests, AMAs and ecosystem distribution were part of a broader acquisition and activation strategy. Working alongside the wider growth and product effort, those programs contributed during a period when the wallet reached roughly 155,000 monthly active users. Product growth was observable. The incremental contribution of any one creator, quest or channel required more careful attribution.

Later, while working on creator-facing growth and distribution for a Bittensor-based network, I saw participating creator accounts represent more than 8 million combined YouTube subscribers and X followers in a June 2026 network snapshot. That's potential distribution capacity, not eight million unique people reached. Views, watch hours and creator activity gave us a more useful picture of actual attention. And even decentralized reward and verification infrastructure still depends on platforms to deliver and measure content.

Start with the behavior, not the personality

Choose the behavior first. An AMA may be designed to help a technical audience understand a new staking product. A quest may encourage a first wallet action. A specialist researcher might earn a qualified conversation with an institutional buyer. These are different assignments, not different ways to buy the same reach.

Different creators can produce different behaviors. An account effective at creating broad awareness may be poor at explaining technical risk. A respected researcher may reach fewer people but influence the exact developers or institutions the project needs.

Evaluate audience relevance in layers

Follower count is potential distribution, not proof of influence. Inspect who actually participates, whether the creator has demonstrated authority on the subject, and whether followers ask substantive questions or take credible next steps. A smaller practitioner audience may have more value than a broad account built around rewards.

Review audience overlap, conflicted sponsorships and the durability of the content before paying for scale. Public interaction patterns and a small paid test can tell you more than a media kit.

Brief for a job, not a talking point

A useful creator brief is not a list of approved slogans. It defines what the content needs to accomplish, which claims can be supported and how the result will be judged.

Creator brief essentials

Five decisions to make before the creator starts.

01 / The job

State the campaign objective, intended buyer and the audience behavior worth producing.

02 / The truth

Explain the real problem, product evidence, approved claims and what must not be promised.

03 / The voice

Share useful links and likely audience questions. Give the creator latitude to explain the product in their own language.

04 / The guardrails

Specify disclosure, non-negotiable boundaries, and a response or escalation contact.

05 / The evidence

Agree on tracking, the observation window and what would justify another campaign.

Illustrative framework

The goal is a creator who can defend the explanation to their own audience, not a paid account reciting the company's copy.

Use a campaign ladder

Don't buy a long-term relationship before you have evidence the creator is right for the job. Treat each engagement as a decision gate, not just another deliverable.

  1. 01
    Qualify

    Relevance test

    Invite the creator to a briefing or product session. Are the questions informed? Does their audience actually overlap with the buyer?

    Advance when the fit is credible and the creator understands the product.

  2. 02
    Activate

    Small experiment

    Run one focused explanation, discussion or event linked to a meaningful audience action.

    Advance when the signal goes beyond impressions or paid responses.

  3. 03
    Evaluate

    Evidence review

    Review relevance, questions, product actions where measurable, and reputational fit. Separate observed behavior from attribution estimates.

    Advance when the evidence supports another investment.

  4. 04
    Compound

    Deeper partnership

    Expand into recurring research, a content series, an event or an ambassador role only after the earlier stages justify it.

    Advance when the relationship delivers repeatable value, not just repeatable posting.

Measure through the funnel

A useful scorecard answers three questions: What did we observe? Which business behavior followed? And what can we responsibly attribute? There is no single metric that answers all three.

Measure the distance from attention to adoption

01 / AttentionDid the right people notice?

Qualified views, audience overlap, watch time and event attendance.

02 / UnderstandingDid the message land?

Relevant questions, product comprehension and changes in recurring confusion.

03 / ActionDid anyone do something useful?

First wallet action, product activation, qualified application or meeting.

04 / PersistenceDid it last beyond the promotion?

Retained cohorts, repeat activity and progress through the buying cycle.

Illustrative framework

Use creator-specific links, event registration, product cohorts and CRM information where appropriate. A click does not automatically connect to an onchain action; privacy-aware event linking can help, but cross-device and assisted influence will remain incomplete. Don't present estimated channel contribution as a verified incremental result.

Include the full cost

Campaign cost is more than the creator fee. Include management time, briefing, product support, creative production, token incentives, event expense, measurement, moderation, and reputational risk.

Then compare the campaign with other credible ways to reach the same audience: direct partnerships, founder content, research, community programs, selective media, or account-based outreach.

Treat disclosure as part of trust

Paid or otherwise material relationships should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission states that a material connection can include payment, free or discounted products, employment, family, or other relationships and that the disclosure should be obvious to the audience.

Projects should provide disclosure requirements in the brief and monitor compliance. A hidden sponsorship may improve short-term aesthetics while damaging the credibility the campaign was supposed to borrow.

The best creator partnership is not the one with the largest screenshot. It is the one in which the right person helps the right audience understand or do something valuable-and both sides can explain the evidence.

lowob takeaway: Buy relevance, authority, and behavior. Reach is only useful when it sits upstream of those outcomes.
